title: What is the Pomodoro technique? Meet the study tomato
description: The Pomodoro technique pairs focused work with breaks. Find out why it has a tomato’s name and how to try a simple study session without chasing a timer.

sections.title: Why is there a tomato on the desk?
sections.html:
The Pomodoro technique is a way to organise focused work and breaks, named after the tomato-shaped kitchen timer used by its creator, Francesco Cirillo.

A surprisingly cheerful name for something that begins with a familiar problem: sitting down to study, then finding twelve other things to do.

sections.title: One student, one kitchen timer
sections.html:
Cirillo says he began developing the method as a university student in the 1980s, when he struggled to concentrate on his studies.

He started by asking whether he could study for a short time without interruption. The tomato was a tool for that experiment, not a special ingredient for a better brain.

sections.title: Give the next task a boundary
sections.html:
Maynooth University’s short guide gives a familiar starting routine: choose one task, work for 25 minutes, then take a five-minute break.

If an unrelated job pops into your head, note it down and return to the task. After four work periods, the guide suggests a longer break.

“Review one page of notes” is a clearer task than “sort out all my studying”.

sections.title: The timer is not keeping score
sections.html:
Cirillo stresses that the full technique goes beyond repeating 25-minute blocks. Planning, interruptions and noticing how you work also matter.

So use the timer as a boundary, not proof that learning happened. After reading, try explaining the idea in your own words, then revisit it later. Those are separate learning steps, not something a ticking tomato can do for you.
